source: FindMyPolitics
population_sample_method: Self-selected online quiz; no survey sample
key_findings: 5 axes (Economic; Social Values; Civil Liberties; Governance globalist-nationalist; System Trust). Quick 30 / Standard 50 / In-Depth 80 items per edition (Global, US); 8 pro + 8 con items per axis. 21 named ideologies. Comparisons to 50 countries and 75 figures; friend comparison; Rooms. Disclosure: Petry wrote all questions, scoring and placements; Claude Code wrote front-end only.
verdict_vs_first_draft: VERIFIED (axis count; lengths; disclosure). Scoring mechanism not on site.
caveats: No methodology/about/FAQ pages exist (links are stubs). No psychometrics. Ideology names rendered client-side.
relevance: Transparency precedent; balanced keying per axis; tiered lengths; comparison hooks.

source: Andrew Yang Podcast: Gen Z Is Rewriting the Political Compass
population_sample_method: 31-36 min interview
key_findings: Description only: Petry; quiz taken by 'hundreds of thousands'; '21 ideologies instead of two parties reveals how much we overlap'.
verdict_vs_first_draft: EXISTS; content UNVERIFIED (no transcript anywhere; audio not accessed)
caveats: Cite nothing beyond the published description.
relevance: Inspiration only.

source: Who Gets a Seat at the Table? (Substack)
population_sample_method: Author blog; self-reported figures
key_findings: 14 to 17 (added Centrist, Democratic Socialism, Fascism) to 21 ideologies. Matching = nearest named point on 5 axes; Centrist is the only exception rule (near zero on all axes). 1 in 28 users mislabelled before the Centrist rule; 21% of prior users relabelled after 17-to-21 change. Every response stores the taxonomy version. Inclusion test: do real people call themselves this; distinct spot on map; explainable fairly with neutral sources. Fascism gated behind 80-item version.
verdict_vs_first_draft: VERIFIED (14 to 21; centrist problem). 'Centroid' is the first draft's word not his.
caveats: Single author; figures unaudited; companion posts robots-blocked and unread.
relevance: Plan a no-match/mixed rule from day one; version every response; expect ~1 in 5 label churn on taxonomy changes; free-text self-ID catches mislabelling.

source: Hidden Tribes: A Study of America's Polarized Landscape
authors_org: More in Common (Hawkins, Yudkin, Juan-Torres, Dixon)
population_sample_method: 8,000 US citizens; YouGov opt-in online panel weighted to 2016 ACS (not probability); 6 focus groups + 30 interviews
key_findings: 7 segments (Progressive Activists 8%, Traditional Liberals 11%, Passive Liberals 15%, Politically Disengaged 26%, Moderates 15%, Traditional Conservatives 19%, Devoted Conservatives 6%). Clustered on core beliefs (group identity, perceived threat, authoritarian disposition, moral foundations, personal agency) plus ideology/activism items; no demographics or party ID in clustering. Gower distance + iterative agglomerative hierarchical clustering; cluster floors ~500 and ceilings ~2,000.
caveats: Opt-in panel; 2017-18 data; website omits N/vendor (PDF has them).
relevance: Cluster on values not issues; 26% disengaged segment is the analogue to expect for AI.

source: Initial validation of the General Attitudes towards AI Scale (GAAIS)
date: 2020-05 (CHB Reports 1:100014); follow-ups 2023 (IJHCI 39:2724) and Short GAAIS-10 (IJHCI online 2026-01)
population_sample_method: 2020: EFA on N=100. 2023: two UK Prolific samples N=304 and N=300. 2026 short form: total N=1,406 incl. representative UK N=500
key_findings: Two factors: Positive (12 items) and Negative (8 items); not bipolar. Latent Pos-Neg r = .40-.48 after reverse scoring. Alphas .85-.88 / .82. Content is sentiment (useful, exciting, sinister, errors), no governance. Correlates: corporate distrust lowers both; introversion raises positivity; openness n.s.; older and female lower Positive.
caveats: Licence is CC BY-NC-ND (2020 and 2023): adapting or commercially embedding items is not clearly permitted; contact authors. 2020 full text not read.
relevance: Benchmark for convergent validity; shows affect is two correlated factors; licence constraint.

source: Whose AI? How different publics think about AI and its social impacts
authors_org: Bao, Krause, Calice, Scheufele, Wirz, Brossard, Newman, Xenos (UW-Madison)
population_sample_method: 'Nationally representative' US, N=2,700; latent class analysis on risk and benefit perceptions
key_findings: 5 classes: Negative (risks > benefits), Ambivalent (high risk AND high benefit), Tepid (slightly more benefit), Ambiguous (moderate both), Indifferent (low both). Classes differ by news attention; 'AI not yet overtly politicized'.
caveats: Class proportions, panel vendor and covariate results UNVERIFIED (paywalled). Data pre-date ChatGPT.
relevance: Risk x benefit grid yields 5 profiles; ambivalence and indifference are real types.

source: Segmenting support for artificial intelligence: Exploring socio-epistemic orientations
population_sample_method: Claimed: quota US web survey N=2,518; LCA 4 profiles
key_findings: Claimed: Optimists / Pessimists / Ambivalent / Indifferent.
verdict_vs_first_draft: UNVERIFIED in full (every access route blocked; no preprint found)
caveats: Not yet verified; nothing in the project relies on it until the abstract and method have been read.
relevance: Candidate 4-class benchmark.

source: How the US Public and AI Experts View Artificial Intelligence
authors_org: Pew Research Center (McClain, Kennedy, Gottfried, Anderson, Pasquini)
population_sample_method: Public: N=5,410 ATP probability panel, Aug 12-18 2024. Experts: N=1,013 US-based, conference-recruited, unweighted, Aug-Oct 2024
key_findings: 56% experts vs 17% public expect very/somewhat positive impact on the US over 20 years. More concerned than excited: public 51% vs experts 15%. ~60% public worry government will not go far enough regulating. Little/no confidence in companies to develop responsibly: public 59%; in government to regulate: 62%. Fewer jobs: public 64% vs experts 39%. Gender gap among experts 63% vs 36% positive.
caveats: Expert sample is a convenience sample.
relevance: Item wording templates (AICHANGE, CNCEXC, AIREG, REGCONF); regulation worry is bipartisan.

source: Americans and AI 2026 (plus Sept 2025 report)
key_findings: 2026: 40% negative vs 16% positive societal impact over 20 years; 63% say AI advancing too quickly; 67% little/no confidence in government regulation (Dem 74, Rep 61; partisan pattern flipped since 2024); ~60% lack confidence in companies; 49% ever use chatbots. 2025: 50% more concerned than excited (37% in 2021), 10% more excited, 38% equal; 57% say societal risks high vs 25% benefits high; 53% expect worse creative thinking; 76% say telling AI content apart is important and 53% not confident they can.
relevance: Current US base rates; the 'equally' middle (38%) is large; trust in regulator tracks who holds power.

source: AI Index Report 2026 ch. 9 Public Opinion (Ipsos AI Monitor 2025 data)
population_sample_method: Ipsos: 30 countries, N=23,216 online adults; 17 countries nationally representative under 75, 12 'connected' urban samples
key_findings: AI Index: 59% benefits > drawbacks (55% in 2024); 52% nervous. Ipsos's own 30-country averages: 56% benefits; 53% nervous; 52% excited; 54% trust own government to regulate. Benefits > drawbacks: Canada 40% (lowest of 30), US 42%, GB 43%, Australia 47%, Indonesia 85% (highest). Nervous: Australia 67%, Canada/US/GB ~61-64%. Excited: Canada 31% (lowest), US 38%, GB 37%, Australia 40%. Trust government to regulate: US 31%, GB 39%, Canada 40%, Australia 46%, Singapore 81%.
verdict_vs_first_draft: VERIFIED as AI Index figures; PARTIAL because they differ from Ipsos's own headline (56/53)
caveats: Country set changes yearly; 12 of 30 samples not representative; chart-read values are approximate. Ipsos 2026 wave (32 countries, N=23,532) reports optimism down in 17 of 28 tracked countries.
relevance: Anglosphere sits in the low-optimism, low-excitement, high-nervousness corner; Canada is the least optimistic.

source: Most adults think AI is developing too fast
population_sample_method: N=2,140 US adults; AmeriSpeak probability panel; MOE ±2.9
key_findings: Too fast 64% / not fast enough 8% / about right 27% (Dem 76, Rep 54). Government priorities, % extremely/very important: keep AI under human control 81; protect US workers 77; minimize environmental harm 69; grow economy 63; promote innovation 51; compete with China 45. Party trusted on AI: neither 39%.
caveats: Topline wording: 'developing too fast, not developing fast enough, or developing at about the right place' (possible typo for 'pace'; check PDF before quoting). No company-vs-government trust item.
relevance: Pace item is a clean discriminator (8% fast); priority ranking supplies item content; human control is near-consensus.

source: What 81
population_sample_method: https://www.anthropic.com/features/81k-interviews
key_findings: N=80,508 completed interviews; 159 countries; 70 languages; all Claude.ai users invited for one week in Dec 2025; interviews conducted by Claude ('Anthropic Interviewer'); Claude classifiers coded responses
verdict_vs_first_draft: Concerns (%): unreliability 26.7; jobs/economy 22.3; autonomy/agency 21.9; cognitive atrophy 16.3; governance 14.7; misinformation 13.6; surveillance/privacy 13.1; malicious use 13.0; meaning/creativity 11.7; overrestriction 11.7; wellbeing/dependency 11.2; sycophancy 10.8; existential risk 6.7; none ~11. 67% net positive. Jobs concern is the strongest predictor of sentiment. Benefits mostly firsthand; harms mostly anticipated.
relevance: Self-selected active users; hopes asked before concerns; non-respondents on concerns filtered out.
column11: Concern vocabulary for item writing (note 'overrestriction' 11.7% and 'autonomy/agency' 21.9%); not a prevalence sample.

source: MFQ-2 (Atari et al. 2023 JPSP; Zakharin & Bates 2023 PAID)
authors_org: Atari, Haidt, Graham, Koleva, Stevens, Dehghani; Zakharin & Bates
population_sample_method: Atari: 25 populations, N=8,672 across 3 studies. Z&B: UK N=809, US N=835, 7-month retest
key_findings: Six foundations (care, equality, proportionality, loyalty, authority, purity); 36 items; retest omega .79-.92; two higher-order factors (individualizing, binding).
verdict_vs_first_draft: VERIFIED (six foundations; 36 items). No MFQ-2 short form found.
caveats: moralfoundations.org hosts only MFQ30/MFQ20 under 'all rights reserved'; MFQ-2 items are in the APA paper/supplement, licence to check. No opened peer-reviewed study links MFQ scores to general AI attitudes (nearest: Maninger & Shank 2022 on judging AI violations; Eriksson et al. 2025/26 'moral framework').
relevance: Do not relabel foundations as AI axes; MFT-AI link is a hypothesis without direct evidence.

source: AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1)
population_sample_method: Voluntary framework
key_findings: Functions Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. Trustworthy characteristics: Valid and Reliable; Safe; Secure and Resilient; Accountable and Transparent; Explainable and Interpretable; Privacy-Enhanced; Fair with Harmful Bias Managed. Generative AI Profile July 2024. NIST page: 'being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan'; April 2026 critical-infrastructure profile concept note.
verdict_vs_first_draft: VERIFIED. No 'AI RMF 2.0' exists; say 'revision underway'.
relevance: Scenario domain coverage only.

source: To Trust or Distrust AI: A Questionnaire Validation Study (FAccT 2025); Visser et al. 2025 (Cognitive Systems Research 101357); Scharowski et al. 2022 position paper
authors_org: Scharowski, Perrig, von Felten, Aeschbach, Opwis, Wintersberger, Brühlmann; Visser, Peters, Scharlau, Hammer
population_sample_method: FAccT: pre-registered online experiment N=1,485. Visser: conceptual review, no sample
key_findings: Jian et al. (2000) trust scale's one-factor model fails; trust and distrust are separate factors that can coexist. Trust (attitude) is distinct from reliance (behaviour) and is system/context specific; explainability-to-trust link not well established.
verdict_vs_first_draft: PARTIAL: the first draft's claim is a synthesis of three papers not a quotation
caveats: PII-to-DOI mapping for Visser plausible but unconfirmed.
relevance: Measure trust and distrust separately; keep trust items context-specific; do not read 'trust' as ideology.

source: U.S. Public Opinion on the Governance of AI (AIES 2020) / American Attitudes and Trends
authors_org: Zhang & Dafoe, Centre for the Governance of AI
population_sample_method: N=2,000 US adults, YouGov, pre-registered
key_findings: 82% say AI should be carefully managed; 41% support development vs 22% oppose. Top governance challenges: data privacy, cyberattacks, surveillance, digital manipulation. Trust to develop: university researchers 50%, US military 49%, civilian government 30%, Facebook 18%. Trust in actors did NOT predict support for development. Age strongest predictor of importance ratings.
relevance: 'Who should govern' and 'which risks' item basis; trust and optimism are separable.

source: What Does the Public Think About AI? (review + AI SHARE database)
authors_org: Dreksler, Law, Ahn, Schiff, Schiff, Peskowitz; GovAI
population_sample_method: Non-systematic review; ~1,800 questions from 218 studies (2014-2023), mostly US/UK
key_findings: 88% of questions measure cognitive constructs, 4% affective; many people hold mixed views; attitudes are application-dependent; knowledge raises both optimism and specific concern; strong wording effects; only 18% of online studies used probability samples. 'Careful management' now 91% US / 92% Europe (2023): near ceiling.
relevance: Best single methods warning; consensus items will not discriminate.

source: Exciting, Useful, Worrying, Futuristic: Public Perception of AI in 8 Countries (AIES 2021)
authors_org: Kelley et al., Google with Ipsos
population_sample_method: N=10,005 across AU, CA, US, KR, FR, BR, IN, NG; online quota panels; open-ends coded
key_findings: Open-end sentiment: worrying dominates in AU/CA/US/FR (30-33%), exciting in IN/BR/NG. Long-term impact: 29% mostly good, 41% 'depends on what happens'. 82% say big tech should weigh pros and cons before release (consistent across countries). No person-level typology.
caveats: Panels not representative esp. BR/IN/NG; pre-ChatGPT.
relevance: The conditional middle ('depends') is the plurality; Canada data point.

source: How do people feel about AI? Wave 2
authors_org: Ada Lovelace Institute & Alan Turing Institute
population_sample_method: N=3,513 UK nationally representative with oversamples; 8 AI uses rated
key_findings: Responsible for safety (up to 3): independent regulator 58%, developing companies 58%, international standards bodies 36%, citizen oversight 31%, ministers 21%; 18-24s prefer companies. Comfort raised by laws 72%, appeal procedures 65%, explanation 61%. 63% not comfortable with AI deciding things affecting them; 62% prefer explanation over accuracy. 50% feel their views are not represented in AI decisions.
relevance: Governance-locus and human-control item wording and base rates; younger people favour companies.

source: Trust
authors_org: attitudes and use of AI: A global study 2025
date: Gillespie, Lockey et al., U. Melbourne with KPMG
population_sample_method: https://mbs.edu/faculty-and-research/trust-and-ai
key_findings: N=48,340 online, 47 countries; each respondent randomised to one AI type
verdict_vs_first_draft: Global: 46% willing to trust AI; 70% say regulation needed. Canada (N=1,025): trust 34% (6th lowest), concern 79%, regulation needed 75%, unaware of Canadian AI laws 92%, AI training 24%. Australia: trust 36%, regulation 77%, safeguards sufficient 30%. Emerging economies higher on trust and adoption.
relevance: UK/US country figures not on accessible pages.
column11: Anglosphere base rates: low trust and high regulation demand.

source: Global Public Opinion on AI (GPO-AI)
authors_org: Schwartz Reisman Institute + PEARL, Munk School (Loewen)
population_sample_method: ~24,000, 21 countries, >1,000 per country, 12 languages
key_findings: 50% support AI development globally; France, US, Canada, UK most negative. Tech companies named as preferred regulators yet only 21% trust them to self-regulate.
caveats: Canada-specific figures not on page; Phase 2 pending.
relevance: Canadian-led dataset; the 'prefer companies but don't trust them' contradiction is quiz-worthy.

source: How people around the world view AI
population_sample_method: N=28,333 across 25 countries plus US
key_findings: Median: more concerned 34%, equally 42%, more excited 16%; US and Australia among highest concern. Trust own country to regulate: US 44% (Rep 54 / Dem 36), India 89%, Greece 22%. Predictors: older and less educated more concerned; heavy internet use more excited.
relevance: Trust in regulator is partisan and anti-establishment coded.

source: Canadian polling 2025-2026 (Leger Aug 2025; Research Co. Jul 2025; Abacus Jul 2025; Angus Reid Oct 2025 & Feb 2026)
authors_org: Leger (N=1,518); Research Co. (N=1,001); Abacus (N=1,915); Angus Reid (N=2,028; 2,020)
population_sample_method: Online panels
key_findings: Leger: 85% want government regulation; good for society 34% / bad 36% / unsure 31%; 83% companies must do more; 78% threatens jobs. Research Co.: threat 50% vs opportunity 37%; slow development 49%, as fast as possible 24%, abandon 13%; trust doctors/nurses 61%, universities 54%, federal gov 38%. Abacus: trust AI 37% vs skeptical 50% (regular users 69%, non-users 5%); 62% expect net job loss.
caveats: Online panels; Angus Reid detail in unopened PDF; no Canadian cluster typology found.
relevance: Canadian base rates: roughly a third each good/bad/unsure; ~1 in 4 'go fast'; usage drives trust.

source: Latent Profiles of AI Risk Perception (Pew ATP W152 reanalysis)
population_sample_method: N=5,255 probability panel; survey-weighted LCA on 9 risk items
key_findings: 4 classes: Concerned Pragmatists 42.8%, Extreme Alarm 29.1%, Moderate Skeptics 17.5%, AI Ambivalent 10.6%. No purely positive class. Demographics explain almost nothing (pseudo-R2 .025).
relevance: Demographics cannot predict type; risk-only items give an ordered concern gradient, not worldviews.

source: AI-Ethics by Design (conjoint + k-means)
population_sample_method: N=1,099 German internet users; conjoint on AI tax-fraud detection with 7 ethical attributes; k=5
key_findings: Importance: accountability > fairness/privacy/security > accuracy > explainability > machine autonomy. Clusters: Ethically Concerned 31%, Indifferent 24%, Safety Concerned 15%, Fairness Concerned 15%, Human in the Loop 14%. Clusters differ by principle priority, not by overall AI attitude.
relevance: Only study found that segments on governance values; supports privacy
column11: fairness and human-control as separable priorities.

source: Ever heard of ethical AI?
population_sample_method: N=14,988 German adults, 15 monthly waves, open-ended
key_findings: 51% not concerned with AI at all; among the concerned, ~15% name ethical issues; fairness/accountability/transparency have almost no spontaneous salience.
relevance: Public does not use governance vocabulary; items must be concrete scenarios.

source: Public Opinion Toward AI (Oxford Handbook chapter)
population_sample_method: Review
key_findings: Attitudes weakly crystallised; high don't-know; large framing effects (facial recognition opposition +16 pts in a year); no general partisan structure; 'AI ethics paradox' (concern without action).
relevance: Expect instability; use scenario-based items.

source: Americans prioritize safety and data security (Gallup-SCSP)
population_sample_method: N=3,128 US adults, Gallup probability panel
key_findings: 80% keep safety rules even if slower; 9% go fast even with fewer rules (Dem 88 / Rep 79 for rules). Who should write rules: US government 54%, companies jointly 53%, each company 16%, none 3%. Who should test before release: independent experts 72%, government 48%, companies 37%. 'Go fast' group much more trusting of AI (56% vs 30%). Development approach: large allied group 42% (Dem 58 / Rep 30), independently 14%.
relevance: Pace is a clean axis with a stable ~10% 'fast' pole; sovereignty vs allies splits by party; pace correlates with trust but is not identical.

source: Ensuring the Consent of the Governed (RAND)
population_sample_method: N=2,000 US adults, nationally representative
key_findings: Among six oversight forms for advanced AI, strongest support for public-private and multinational partnerships; strong support for oversight of the most powerful systems.
relevance: Governance-locus options for items.

source: Governing Artificial Intelligence: Public Preferences and Regulatory Options (conjoint)
population_sample_method: 7 countries (BR, CN, DE, IN, ZA, UK, US), N=14,239; 9 paired tasks; attributes safety vs innovation, government vs firms, national vs international
key_findings: Safety over innovation ~12-point choice gap (~4x the other attributes). Government regulation preferred in CN, DE, UK, US. International preferred in BR, DE, IN, ZA, UK; China prefers national; US no clear preference.
relevance: Conjoint attribute template; sovereignty axis has country-dependent sign.

source: Reduced AI Acceptance After the GenAI Boom
authors_org: Baumann, Urman, Leicht-Deobald, Roman, Hannák, Christen
population_sample_method: Switzerland, two cross-sections N=1,514 (2022) and 1,488 (2023), weighted
key_findings: Acceptance of AI decisions fell in 5 of 7 scenarios; 'human only' rose 18.0% to 25.5%; 'AI only' flat ~7-8%; political orientation and digital literacy had no effect.
relevance: Aggregate attitudes moved materially around ChatGPT; human-control axis is live.

source: NAIOM Report 04 (Rutgers)
population_sample_method: N=5,154 US adults, PureSpectrum nonprobability quotas, reweighted
key_findings: 59% strict regulation vs 25% minimal; <1 in 10 would let AI make final unsupervised decisions on hiring, loans, admissions, parole, medical priority; 45-54% say AI should not be used at all for those; ~76% want employers to disclose AI evaluation. Confidence that AI acts in public interest flipped by party.
relevance: Human-control base rates by decision domain.

source: Pace/pause polling (AIPI/YouGov 2023; FLI 2025; ControlAI/YouGov UK 2025; Public Citizen memo 2026)
authors_org: AI Policy Institute; Future of Life Institute; ControlAI; Public Citizen
population_sample_method: AIPI N=1,001 and 1,118 US voters; FLI N=2,000 US; ControlAI N=2,344 UK; Public Citizen memo aggregates polls without Ns
key_findings: AIPI 2023: slow 72% vs speed up 8%; 47% oppose open-sourcing powerful models vs 23% support. FLI 2025: 64% say no superhuman AI until proven safe or never; 5% develop ASAP. ControlAI UK: halt rapid superintelligence 73%; liability 82%. Public Citizen memo lists 2026 polls at 66-71% 'too fast' and 63-75% opposing local data centres (leads to verify).
caveats: All sponsors are advocacy organisations; framing-sensitive.
relevance: 'Go fast' pole is 5-10% in advocacy polls, ~24% in neutral Canadian poll: framing matters. Only one general-population open-weights poll exists (2023, US).

source: ATTARI-12 (Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence)
population_sample_method: German samples; Study 2 N=150 retest
key_findings: 12-item unidimensional general attitude scale; test-retest r = .80 over ~31 days; wording (acquiescence) factor ~21% of common variance; social desirability r = .04.
relevance: Only direct AI-attitude retest figure found; benchmark for stability gate; balanced keying matters.

source: Public acceptance of various ways to use and treat AI: a predictive moral framework
population_sample_method: N=589 US Prolific quota; 100 AI applications; preregistered
key_findings: Five moral qualities (risk, benefit, dishonesty, unnaturalness, reduced accountability) relatively independent (mean |r| .26). Risk + benefit explain 69.6% of application acceptability; all five explain 91.4%.
relevance: Direct evidence that risk/benefit alone is insufficient; dishonesty and accountability add explanatory power.

source: AIAS-4 (AI Attitude Scale)
population_sample_method: N=230 UK EFA + N=300 US CFA, Prolific
key_findings: Initial items split into personal-benefit and social-risk factors (r = .75); one-factor scale after dropping an item; author says societal risk needs separate measurement.
relevance: Personal attitude is one factor; societal risk partly separable.

source: Existing AI-compass quizzes online
authors_org: Bloomberg Opinion 'AI-dentities' (2025); Keaton's AI Future Compass; AI Safety Compass; doom-or-bloom.com; Telegraph 'Doomer or Zoomer' (2024); Tercek tech-optimism self-score
population_sample_method: None publish methodology or psychometrics
key_findings: All are 1-2 axes (doom-bloom; regulate-or-not; open-closed; safety-first vs risk-skeptic), US-centric, anchored on elite figures (Yudkowsky, LeCun, Altman, Amodei). Bloomberg: 12 questions, six 'AI-dentities', implied optimism x regulation 2x2.
relevance: Differentiation: published items
column12: versioning and Anglosphere base rates would be new.

source: Best practices for developing and validating scales
authors_org: Boateng, Neilands, Frongillo, Melgar-Quiñonez, Young (Frontiers in Public Health 6:149)
population_sample_method: Methods review
key_findings: 9 steps in 3 phases; item pool >= 2x final; 5-7 point scales; N 10 per item or 200-300 overall; parallel analysis not eigenvalue>1; loadings >= .40; item-total >= .30; CFA CFI/TLI >= .95, RMSEA <= .06, SRMR <= .08; alpha .70 accepted in practice (Nunnally .80 for research).
caveats: Authors label most cutoffs rules of thumb.
relevance: Gate table source.

source: Ten frequently asked questions about latent class analysis; LCA best-practice guide; systematic review of LCA practice
authors_org: Nylund-Gibson & Choi 2018; Weller, Bowen & Faubert 2020; Sorgente et al. 2025 (BRM 57:301)
population_sample_method: Methods
key_findings: BIC most trusted plus BLRT; entropy >= .80 is classification quality, never a selection criterion; smallest class >= 5% conventional; N 300-1,000 for indices to behave; 3-step covariate approach; external validation rarely done (split-half in 3.8% of studies).
relevance: Gate table source.

source: Non-attitudes and multi-item stability
authors_org: Converse 1964 via Smith 1981 (NORC); Achen 1975; Zaller 1992; Ansolabehere, Rodden & Snyder 2008; Gerber et al. 2026 panel
population_sample_method: Panel studies and theory
key_findings: Single issue items correlate .3-.5 over two years; about half the variance is noise; averaging many items brings stability toward party-ID levels; modern 6-month panel: party ID .97, ideology .95, stereotype scales .45-.53. No general-population panel on AI governance attitudes exists.
caveats: AI-specific stability unknown beyond ATTARI r=.80 at one month.
relevance: Expect single AI items to be unstable; score multi-item dimensions; retest subsample is the project's own first evidence.

source: Barnum effect; type-based instrument critiques; acquiescence; midpoints; order effects
authors_org: Dickson & Kelly 1985; Randall et al. 2017 (MBTI meta-analysis); Stein & Swan 2019; Savalei & Falk 2014; Billiet & Davidov 2008; Menold 2020; Sturgis et al. 2014; Krosnick 2002; Stark et al. 2018
population_sample_method: Experiments and reviews
key_findings: Vague favourable profiles rated accurate (Forer M=4.3/5): user accuracy ratings are not validity. MBTI dimension retest .61-.78; types unimodal not bimodal. Acquiescence is a stable trait: balance keying. Double-barreled items break invariance. Only 13-25% of midpoint answers are genuine middle opinions; explicit DK options raise no-opinion without improving reliability. Order effects arise when same-topic items are adjacent: randomize.
relevance: Use a shuffled-type control; score dimensions and derive types; no explicit DK on core items but a labelled midpoint plus confidence probe.

source: Cognitive interviewing guidance
authors_org: GESIS guide; ISR/SRC 2007; Blair & Conrad 2011 (POQ 75:636); Beatty & Willis 2007
population_sample_method: Methods
key_findings: Think-aloud vs verbal probing; 10-20 per round typical; Blair & Conrad: n=5 finds <25% of problems, n=15 ~45%, n=20 ~50%, n=50 ~80%; recommend >= 2 rounds of ~25; two coders kappa >= .61.
caveats: Round count is convention; sample-size curve is empirical.
relevance: Plan 2 rounds, 12-15 minimum, 25 target.

source: Conjoint design and power
authors_org: Hainmueller, Hopkins & Yamamoto 2014; Stefanelli & Lukac 2020; Rudolph, Freitag & Thurner 2024
population_sample_method: Methods and simulation
key_findings: AMCE identified under randomization; sign/magnitude errors common below ~3,000 profile observations, >15 levels, or effects < .03; attribute order does not bias weighting.
relevance: A 5-task conjoint at N=300 reaches the 3,000-observation floor; subgroup contrasts need N >= 1,000.

source: When Will AI Transform Society? Swedish Public Predictions on AI Development Timelines
population_sample_method: Probability sample of Swedish adults, n=1,026 (25% response), mixed mode
key_findings: Latent class on five expected-outcome items: Optimists 47%, Ambivalents 42%, Skeptics 11% (low probability for good and bad outcomes alike).
caveats: Single country; binary items; the skeptic class is low-expectation, not high-harm.
relevance: Supports a low-benefit perspective (Skeptics, taxonomy 0.3.0).

source: Americans Cool Toward AI (Bentley-Gallup Business in Society)
population_sample_method: Gallup Panel, probability-based web, n=3,270 US adults
key_findings: More harm than good 39% (31% in 2025), equal 52%, more good 9%; ages 18–29 more harm 47%; 79% expect fewer US jobs.
relevance: Size of the skeptic share and its growth; Skeptics rationale.

source: The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions

key_findings: Six factions: effective accelerationists and the tech right; populist right; safetyists; effective altruists; AI ethics; AI as a normal technology.
caveats: Elite factions defined by named people, not public segments.
relevance: Source for the "Elsewhere you might hear" lines.
